description: SGV 626 Eats regional cuisine taxonomy. ~20 regions grouped into geographic families. Each restaurant gets one primary and optionally one secondary cuisine.

regions.name: Cantonese
regions.description: The most internationally recognized Chinese cuisine, built around fresh ingredients, delicate seasoning, and masterful technique. Rooted in Guangzhou and the Pearl River Delta. The culinary backbone of the SGV.
regions.flavorProfile: Delicate, clean, umami-rich, lightly seasoned
keyDishes: Steamed fish with ginger and scallion
regions.notes: Excludes dim sum and roast meat shops, which have their own categories below. Full-service restaurants serving cooked Cantonese dishes.

regions.name: Dim Sum
regions.description: The Cantonese tradition of yum cha — tea house dining with steamed, fried, and baked small plates served from rolling carts or ordered by form. A weekend ritual in the SGV.
regions.flavorProfile: Varied — delicate, savory, crispy, sticky
keyDishes: Lo mai gai (sticky rice in lotus leaf)
regions.notes: Assign this when dim sum is the restaurant's primary or defining format, even if they also serve dinner.

regions.name: Teochew
regions.description: Cuisine of the Chaoshan region of eastern Guangdong. Closely related to Cantonese but distinct — lighter seasoning, fermented ingredients (especially preserved vegetables and fish sauce), and a strong tradition of cold marinated meats and seafood.
regions.flavorProfile: Light, clean, with salty-fermented depth and natural sweetness
regions.notes: Also spelled Chaozhou or Chiuchow. Distinct from Cantonese despite being from the same province.

regions.name: Hakka
regions.description: The cuisine of the Hakka people, who migrated from northern China into Guangdong and beyond over centuries. Hearty, rustic cooking with mountain influences — braised meats, stuffed tofu, and preserved vegetables.
regions.flavorProfile: Savory, hearty, earthy, braised-forward
keyDishes: Pork belly with preserved vegetables (梅菜扣肉)
regions.notes: Distinct from both Cantonese and Teochew. Often found in dedicated Hakka restaurants rather than general Cantonese menus.

regions.name: Hong Kong Style
regions.description: The distinct culinary culture of Hong Kong — cha chaan teng (Hong Kong-style diners) blending Cantonese tradition with Western and colonial influences. Milk tea, pineapple buns, HK-style French toast, and wonton noodles served in a fast-casual setting.
regions.flavorProfile: Eclectic — silky milk tea, sweet-savory baked goods, umami noodles
regions.notes: Assign when the restaurant's identity is specifically Hong Kong café/diner culture, not just general Cantonese.

regions.name: Shanghainese
regions.description: The cuisine of Shanghai — characterized by a sweet-savory balance (using sugar liberally), rich red-braised dishes, fresh seafood, and the world-famous xiaolongbao (soup dumplings). The Jiangnan culinary tradition at its most refined.
regions.flavorProfile: Sweet-savory, rich, umami-forward, delicate when steamed
regions.notes: Often the primary or sole cuisine of a restaurant. The xiaolongbao is the signature identifier.

regions.name: Jiangsu & Zhejiang
regions.description: The refined cuisines of Hangzhou, Suzhou, Ningbo, and surrounding Jiangnan region. Delicate, seasonal, and elegant — famous for Dongpo pork, West Lake vinegar fish, and Ningbo-style glutinous rice balls.
regions.flavorProfile: Delicate, seasonal, mild sweet-savory, freshwater fish
keyDishes: West Lake vinegar fish (西湖醋鱼)
regions.notes: Distinct from Shanghainese. Use when the restaurant specifically features Hangzhou or Ningbo cuisine.

regions.name: Sichuan
regions.description: Chengdu-centered cuisine defined by the iconic mala (麻辣) flavor — the numbing tingle of Sichuan peppercorn combined with fiery chili. One of the most globally influential regional cuisines.
regions.flavorProfile: Mala (numbing-spicy), bold, aromatic, deeply savory
keyDishes: Boiled fish in chili oil (水煮鱼)
regions.notes: Chengdu-style. For Chongqing-specific hot pot or extreme heat, use the chongqing category.

regions.name: Chongqing
regions.description: The cuisine of the Yangtze River city of Chongqing — significantly hotter than Chengdu Sichuan, with a more aggressive chili-forward heat profile. Home of the original mala hot pot and Chongqing noodles.
regions.flavorProfile: Intensely spicy, aggressive chili heat, bold and oily
regions.notes: Use specifically for restaurants self-identifying as Chongqing style. Chongqing hot pot uses more tallow-based broth and is distinct from Sichuan mala pot.

regions.name: Hunan
regions.description: The cuisine of Hunan province — spicy like Sichuan but without the numbing peppercorn. Hunan heat is pure, direct, and often combined with preserved or smoked meats. Chopped chili (剁椒) is the defining condiment.
regions.flavorProfile: Pure spicy heat, smoky, sour-savory, preserved ingredients
keyDishes: Chopped chili fish head (剁椒鱼头)
Chairman Mao's braised pork (毛氏红烧肉)
regions.notes: Key distinction from Sichuan: no Sichuan peppercorn, different heat character.

regions.name: Yunnan
regions.description: The diverse cuisine of China's most biodiverse province — crossroads of Southeast Asia, Tibet, and Han China. Famous for crossing-the-bridge rice noodles, wild mushrooms, and unique minority ethnic flavors.
regions.flavorProfile: Herbal, floral, earthy (mushrooms), mild-to-medium spice, sour notes
regions.notes: Increasingly popular in SGV. Mushroom hot pot is a distinctive identifier.

regions.name: Guizhou & Guangxi
regions.description: The cuisines of Guizhou (sour-spicy, heavily fermented) and Guangxi (rice noodle hub, Southeast Asian influence). Luosifen (snail noodles from Liuzhou, Guangxi) has become internationally trendy. Guizhou is known for sour soup fish.
regions.flavorProfile: Sour, spicy, fermented, funky, herbaceous
regions.notes: Most SGV representatives are snail noodle shops. Genuine Guizhou restaurants are very rare.

regions.name: Beijing & Northern
regions.description: The imperial cuisine of Beijing and broader northern China — Peking duck, moo shu pork, zhajiangmian (wheat noodles in fermented bean sauce), and jianbing street pancakes. Wheat-forward, with hearty warming dishes.
regions.flavorProfile: Savory-sweet, wheat-based, roasted, fermented bean paste
regions.notes: Peking duck restaurants are the most common representative in SGV.

regions.name: Dongbei
regions.description: The hearty cuisine of China's northeastern provinces (Heilongjiang, Jilin, Liaoning) — influenced by Korean, Russian, and Manchu traditions. Big portions, rich pork-forward dishes, and the characteristic use of sauerkraut.
regions.flavorProfile: Hearty, rich, pork-forward, sauerkraut, starchy
keyDishes: Di san xian (地三鲜 — potato, eggplant, pepper)
Guo bao rou (锅包肉 — sweet-sour fried pork)
regions.notes: Strong Korean influence in some dishes. Often large shared-format plates.

regions.name: Xinjiang
regions.description: The cuisine of China's westernmost region — predominantly Uyghur, with strong Central Asian influence. Lamb is the defining protein, cumin is the signature spice, and flatbread (naan) is served with everything.
regions.flavorProfile: Cumin-forward, lamb, smoky, mildly spiced, Central Asian
regions.notes: Most Xinjiang restaurants are halal. Big plate chicken is the most common SGV representative dish.

regions.name: Shaanxi & Lanzhou
regions.description: The noodle-centric cuisines of northwest China. Xi'an (Shaanxi) brings biang biang noodles, roujiamo (Chinese burger), and the famous paomo lamb soup. Lanzhou is home to the hand-pulled Lanzhou beef noodle soup, now found worldwide.
regions.flavorProfile: Bold, cumin-tinged, hand-pulled noodles, lamb and beef
keyDishes: Lanzhou beef noodle soup (兰州拉面)
regions.notes: Many dedicated Lanzhou beef noodle shops in SGV. Xi'an Famous Foods popularized this category in the US.

regions.name: Taiwanese
regions.description: The distinctive cuisine of Taiwan — a blend of Fujianese, Japanese, and indigenous influences. Beef noodle soup, braised pork rice (lu rou fan), and oyster vermicelli are the iconic trinity. Night market street food culture is central.
regions.flavorProfile: Sweet-savory soy, five-spice braised, mild, comfort-forward
keyDishes: Lu rou fan (braised pork rice 卤肉饭)
regions.notes: Very well represented in SGV. Taiwanese breakfast shops are also a sub-category.

regions.name: Hot Pot
regions.description: Communal cooking at the table in a simmering broth. The experience varies dramatically by broth style — use sub-styles to distinguish. For classification purposes: if hot pot is the restaurant's primary format, assign this category regardless of regional origin.
regions.flavorProfile: Varies by broth: mala (numbing-spicy) / clear (delicate) / tomato / mushroom (earthy)
regions.notes: Assign HOT POT when it is the main format. If a restaurant is primarily Cantonese but happens to offer a hot pot, classify it as Cantonese. The hot pot category is for dedicated hot pot restaurants.

regions.name: Cantonese BBQ
regions.description: The Cantonese roasted meats tradition — the char siu (BBQ pork), roast duck, soy sauce chicken, and crispy pork belly hanging in restaurant windows. A dedicated culinary craft distinct from full-service Cantonese dining.
regions.flavorProfile: Sweet-savory caramelized glaze, smoky roasted, lacquered
keyDishes: Crispy roast pork belly (脆皮烧肉)
regions.notes: Use when the restaurant is primarily a roast meat shop or the menu is centered on roasted meats over rice.

regions.name: Modern & Fusion
regions.description: Contemporary Chinese cuisine that transcends regional boundaries — creative tasting menus, ABC (American-Born Chinese) comfort food, innovative interpretations of classic dishes, or restaurants deliberately blending multiple regional cuisines without one defining identity.
regions.flavorProfile: Varied — creative, modern, often familiar-but-elevated
regions.notes: Use as a last resort. Most restaurants can be classified into a specific regional cuisine if enough data is available.
